query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered suitable for thin-film use, and its expense favors applying it as a protective coating on conventional metals rather than using it in bulk. Earlier studies examined room-temperature wear behavior in relation to coating–substrate combinations, composition, and grain size, but largely addressed the alloy itself or a limited thermal regime rather than the overall wear response of a coating across different temperatures. Under the constraints that FeNiCrCoCu remains a thin protective coating and that high-temperature wear is the target application, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its overall wear resistance and why? Specify an intervention relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, state the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The high-temperature wear resistance of FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings is governed by the formation of a stable oxide layer on the surface, which acts as a lubricant and reduces the friction coefficient and specific wear rate.
generation.material_initial_state: FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coating on a conventional metal substrate
generation.intervention: In-situ high-temperature tribometry with simultaneous microstructural characterization
generation.conditions: High-temperature wear regime, with temperatures ranging from 500°C to 900°C
generation.structural_mediator: Stable oxide layer formation on the surface
generation.mechanism: Lubrication effect of the oxide layer, reducing friction coefficient and specific wear rate
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved wear resistance and reduced friction coefficient at high temperatures
generation.baseline: Room-temperature wear behavior of FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coating
generation.boundary: Temperature range of 500°C to 900°C, and normal load range of 10-50 N
generation.uncertainty: The exact composition and microstructure of the oxide layer, and its effect on the wear resistance and friction coefficient

falsification_experiment.design: In-situ high-temperature tribometry with simultaneous microstructural characterization, using a FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coating on a conventional metal substrate
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxide layer formation is suppressed, and the friction coefficient and specific wear rate do not decrease with increasing temperature, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.kind: web:3.1. Phase Structure and Morphology of CoCrFeNiMn High-Entropy Alloy Coating
cited_evidence.text: Figure 7 shows the microhardness distribution curves of CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy coatings prepared by CS and HVOF, and the coatings heat-treated at different temperatures. Both coatings reach the highest hardness at 500 °C, 487.6 HV0.1 for CS coating and 352.4 HV0.1 for HVOF coating. At 700 °C and 900 °C, the hardness of both coatings is lower than that at room temperature. This is because the heat treatment at 500 °C makes the coating form a heterogeneous structure composed of nanotwins in the recrystallized grains, and high-density dislocations appear in the deformation region. When the annealing temperature exceeds 500 °C, the coating exhibits a completely recrystallized structure, the yield stress decreases and the hardness decreases.

Both sliding speed and normal load will affect the friction and wear behavior of the different grain size CoCrFeMnNi HEAs. Increasing the sliding speed will increase the friction coefficient and specific wear rate of the alloy. Thus, increase the normal load, reduce the friction coefficient, and decrease the specific wear rate of the alloy. This is because the oxide layer formed on the worn surface under high load plays a role in lubrication and reduces the friction coefficient and specific wear rate.
